This is the same dataset used in the chapter. Each row is one country and each column is one measurement recorded about that country, such as its name, its region of the world, its population, and its life expectancy.
One note about the code that loaded the data. The variable ub was set in the setup to the web address where the course files live. Adding it in front of a file name lets Colab download the file before reading it. You do not need to think about ub beyond that.

Look at the output from the previous question. Polars prints the size of the dataset at the top. How many observations (rows) and how many variables (columns) does it have?

Answer: There are 135 observations and 15 variables. The book calls a row an observation and a column a variable, so this dataset records 15 measurements for each of 135 countries.

In your own words, what does a single row of this dataset represent, and what does a single column represent?

Answer: A single row represents one country, together with everything we measured about it. A single column represents one measurement, such as population or life expectancy, recorded across every country in the dataset.

Read the size of the food dataset from its output. How many rows and columns does it have?

Answer: It has 61 rows and 17 columns, so the book records 17 variables about each of 61 food items.

Look at the short labels printed just under the column names in the country output, such as str, i64, and f64. These are the data types. Columns of text are marked str, and columns of numbers are marked i64 or f64. Name one text column and one number column.

Answer: Text columns include full_name, region, and lang. Number columns include pop, lexp, and gdp. We will look at what the different number types mean later in the course; for now it is enough to tell text from numbers.

The chapter lists a few rules for formatting code. One rule is to put a single space before and after the equals sign and around math operators. The line below breaks that rule. Rewrite it with correct spacing.



View code
pop=45* 2




View code
pop = 45 * 2



Another rule is to name variables with lowercase letters and underscores, and to start every name with a letter. Of the four names below, which two follow the book’s advice?

MyData      my_data      2nd_country      country_pop
Answer: my_data and country_pop follow the advice: both are lowercase with underscores and both start with a letter. MyData uses capital letters, which the book recommends against, and 2nd_country starts with a number, which Python does not allow at all.
That is the whole notebook. Starting next time, we will begin reshaping and sorting datasets rather than just looking at them.

title: Notebook01
text:
Setup
Run all of the following before starting the notebook.


View code
! wget -q -nc https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taylor-arnold/fds2/refs/heads/main/funs.py




View code
import polars as pl
from plotnine import ggplot, aes
from polars import col as c

import funs

ub = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/taylor-arnold/fds2/refs/heads/main/"




Questions
Welcome to the first notebook. The goal today is just to get comfortable running code, so every question is short. Each gray box is a code cell: click into it and press Shift+Enter to run it. The result shows up right below. To see the result of something, type it into a cell and run it.
We will start by using Python as a calculator, then create a few variables, and finish with our first function.

Add the numbers 8 and 15.



View code
8 + 15


23



There are 24 hours in a day. Multiply to find how many hours are in a week of 7 days.



View code
24 * 7


168



Python follows the usual order of operations, and parentheses let you control it. Run the expression below and check that the answer is what you expected.



View code
(20 - 5) / 3


5.0



Instead of just looking at a result, we can store it. Create a variable named mynum that holds the value of 3 + 5.



View code
mynum = 3 + 5



Nothing appeared below the cell in the previous question. Why not?

Answer: The result was saved into the variable mynum instead of being displayed. Storing a value and showing a value are two different things: an assignment with = keeps the result for later but does not print it.

Now use your variable. Add 1 to mynum.



View code
mynum + 1


9



You can have as many variables as you like and combine them. Create a variable width equal to 4 and a variable height equal to 7, then multiply them together to get the area.



View code
width = 4
height = 7
width * height


28



Time for our first function. The round function takes a number and returns the nearest whole number. Round the value 2.71828.



View code
round(2.71828)


3



Most functions accept more than one input. Give round a second number to say how many digits to keep. Round 2.71828 to 2 digits.



View code
round(2.71828, 2)


2.72



We can also pass inputs by name, which makes the code easier to read. Round 2.71828 to 3 digits using the argument names number and ndigits.



View code
round(number=2.71828, ndigits=3)


2.718


That is the whole notebook. Next time we will load a real dataset and start looking at it.
